entities.summary:
Victor Hugo (1802–1885) was a French poet, novelist, and dramatist who dominated French literature for over sixty years. His novels 'Les Misérables' (1862) and 'The Hunchback of Notre-Dame' (1831) are among the most widely read works in world literature, and his poetry collections established him as France's greatest Romantic poet.

Hugo's literary career began early—he published his first poetry collection at 20 and his play 'Hernani' (1830) triggered a battle between Classicists and Romantics that defined French cultural politics. His preface to 'Cromwell' (1827) became the manifesto of the French Romantic movement.

A fierce republican, Hugo spent 19 years in political exile (1851–1870) on the Channel Islands after opposing Napoleon III's coup d'état. During exile he wrote 'Les Misérables,' whose portrayal of poverty, injustice, and redemption made it one of the most influential novels ever written.

Hugo's funeral in 1885 drew two million mourners—the largest public gathering in French history to that date. His advocacy for the abolition of the death penalty, universal suffrage, and free education made him a prophet of social justice. As André Gide quipped when asked to name France's greatest poet: 'Victor Hugo—hélas!'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Victor Hugo's works had a profound impact on world literature, with 'Les Misérables' being adapted into numerous stage productions and films, and his poetry collections influencing the development of Romanticism. His exile and advocacy for republicanism also shaped French politics.
